job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Pedro Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up early for football on Tuesdays and Thursdays, otherwise it's the Brantford Polytechnic workshop by nine. I'm doing a master's in mechatronics after my mechanical engineering degree, so I'm in the lab with a small robot arm that sorts parts on a belt. My internship last summer was three months at Orrin Packaging, which builds machines that wrap boxes. I rent a room in a student house, and my dad's tyre shop can't help with money, so I owe about 29,000 and I'm always checking the balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I thought. A few routine tasks get quicker, but a machine on a belt still needs someone who understands the machine. I'd joke at football that my degree is safe, and then go back to counting how much I owe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's neutral for me. The job market near Brantford is thin, with Orrin Packaging and two or three other plants, and they hire a graduate every year or two. So the real question is whether one of those chairs is free when I finish, and AI has nothing to do with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, and send applications to every plant in two hours' drive, about 25 of them. I'd ask Orrin for a summer contract, since they liked my work. And I'd keep my weekend job at the garage with my dad, changing tyres, which pays cash and keeps me honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty steady. A bit nervous about the interviews, but I like the work and I'm not afraid of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which jobs near you suit a mechatronics graduate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit for the boring things. I ask an assistant to write the small scripts that talk to the robot arm, then I check them line by line. It saves me an hour on a bad day, but it also gets things wrong, so I never trust it with the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use AI for now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Orrin, a bottling plant called Kessler, and a company that makes lifts. About four graduate jobs a year across all of them, I'd say. It's a lot of us going after very few chairs.

say: I'd joke at football that my **degree is safe**, then go back to counting what I owe.
I'd say a machine on a belt still needs **someone who understands it**.
think: It's neutral for me: the real question is whether a **chair is free** at one of the plants.
There are about **four graduate jobs** a year nearby.
do: Send **25 applications** to plants within two hours' drive.
Ask Orrin for a **summer contract**, and keep my tyre-changing weekend job with my dad.
feel: **Steady**, a bit nervous about interviews but fine with the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, but the machines on the factory floor are still metal, and somebody has to put them in. I'd tell my mates the thinking part, like drawing and calculating, will change first, and the hands-on part later. I'd say learn both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the design side of my job gets squeezed. At Orrin I spent most of my time in CAD, the drawing software, and writing calculations. If an AI does the first draft, a firm like Orrin needs one designer where it needed three. But a mechatronics person who can also commission the machine, I think that's still needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get more serious with the AI tools, maybe use them for every script and drawing check for six months and see where they fail. I'd ask Orrin about the commissioning team, the people who install and test machines on site. And I'd keep the tyre weekends, because cash on hand is a good friend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert, rather than scared. A bit like the minute before a match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks in a machine design job would AI take on first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Drawing parts, doing the load calculations and writing the test reports. My supervisor, Marta, said she could draw a bracket in forty minutes and the AI did it in four. She was kind of laughing, but not completely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him that it's fine, that I'm working on it. His shop isn't touched by AI yet, but his customers are, and he's worried about the car trade changing. I'd want him to hear I'm planning, not panicking.

say: I'd tell mates the **thinking part** changes first and the hands-on part later, so learn both.
I'd say the machines are still **metal** and someone has to install them.
think: The design side gets squeezed: one designer where they needed **three**.
A mechatronics person who can **commission** the machine is still needed.
do: Use AI on **every script** for six months to see where it fails.
Ask Orrin about the **commissioning team**, and keep the tyre weekends.
feel: **Alert, not scared**, like the minute before a match.

steps.text: Use an AI tool for every script and drawing check for six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow down and plan, because two years isn't enough for a town like Brantford. I'd say it at football, at the pub and anywhere else. But I'd also say we shouldn't ban it, because the machines could do good things too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be frightened for my dad, not only for myself. My dad's tyre shop runs on thin margins, and if Brantford loses its plants, nobody has money for tyres. And my first job vanishes, and with it the thing that might have helped pay the shop's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the master's if there were no way to land a job, though I'd probably finish it because of the loan. I'd start picking up as many shifts at the garage as I can, and look for a trade licence in mechanical or electrical work. And I'd talk to my dad about whether the shop can stay open if I help full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened and sort of angry. I keep thinking about the shop lights going off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most about your own family in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop. If his takings drop, I'd have to send money I don't have. I'd probably borrow more, and then I'm in a spiral nobody would call good planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad first, then my uncle Karim, who's a plumber and knows how to get work in a downturn. I'd ask him how people got through the last big factory closure. Not a lot of wisdom there, I'd guess, but it's something.

say: I'd say we need to **slow down and plan**, but not ban it, because machines could do good.
I'd say it at football and at the pub, to anyone.
think: I'm frightened for my **dad's tyre shop**, which runs on thin margins and a few customers.
If the town loses its plants, nobody can pay for tyres and my **first job** vanishes too.

feel: **Frightened and angry**, picturing the shop lights going off.

fieldNote: Pedro's fear is about the **household earner**, his dad, more than himself.

steps.text: Work extra shifts at the tyre shop to help my dad keep it open
Look into a trade licence in mechanical or electrical work

Apply for any hands-on job at the plants, even on the line

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is the sweet spot for planning. It's enough to retrain people and short enough that people take it seriously. I'd tell the regional council to start now, not wait for a report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd see an opening. If thinking AI arrives by 2031 and robots by 2034, someone has to design and fit the robots, and that's me. I might even do well, because mechatronics is the field of building them. But the pay may be squeezed, and I'd worry about timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first mechatronics or maintenance job I can, save about 200 a month and pay down the loan. I'd learn to use the AI tools properly, because my work will be to put them into machines. And I'd try to get a second skill, like PLC programming, the logic that runs a factory line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, a bit anxious. Mostly it feels like a race I can win if I start early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd keep mechatronics. If I picked something purely thinking-based, like pure software, I'd be in the line of fire. Mechatronics has a hand in the real world, and I like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a different master's today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Orrin might do well or badly. If they build robots, they'd hire. If they buy robots from somewhere else, they wouldn't. I'd keep an eye on both outcomes and apply widely.

I'd say don't wait for a report.

Pay may be squeezed and **timing** is the risk.

steps.text: Take the first maintenance or mechatronics job offered near Brantford
Put 200 a month toward the loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news that there's time. Ten years can fix a lot if people act: training, savings, new rules. I'd tell my friends to get on with their lives, and not to freeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd honestly feel good. I'd have time to pay off the debt, get a few years in a good plant and maybe move to a bigger city. By 2036 I'd be 34 and somebody who knows both the machines and the tools. If the robots come around 2039, I'm the one who knows how to service them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first job, then try to move into automation design within three years. I'd pay the loan down to nothing by around 30 and save for a place of my own. I'd also keep helping at my dad's shop whenever it's busy, because it keeps me close to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relaxed, with a bit of pride. I like the idea of being on the right side of the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn something you can do with your hands and your head, and don't count on one employer. And play football. It helps with everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger brother about careers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also say to keep one eye on money. Most trouble I've seen was about money, not technology.

I'd push for training, savings and new rules over the next decade.
think: I'd honestly feel good: by 2036 I'd be **34** and know both the machines and the tools.

feel: **Relaxed** with some pride at being on the right side of the robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. It leaves me no time and puts my dad's shop at risk as well. What would help is retraining that comes with a wage, a plan for towns that lose their plants, and loan relief if a degree stops paying.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that I've felt more hopeful than I expected. Thinking of my own field as the one that builds the robots, not the one replaced by them, helped me a lot. Whether that's true, I don't know.

headlineQuote: Thinking of my own field as the one that builds the robots, not the one replaced by them, helped me a lot.
portrait: Pedro is 24, doing a **mechatronics master's** after mechanical engineering, with 29,000 of debt and a dad whose tyre shop is struggling.
He did a three-month internship at a packaging machine maker and changes tyres on weekends for cash.
He is centrist and practical, uses AI **now and then**, and checks every line.
His moods run anxious to uneasy, jumping to alarmed at two years, when his dad's shop is at risk.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which leaves no time and puts his dad's shop at risk.
whatWouldHelp: He wants retraining **with a wage**, a plan for towns that lose plants and loan relief.
